title: Week 3 Quiz — Revolution, Independence, and Competing Liberties

republicanism
questions.explanation: republicanism is defined in this week as: The belief that government should serve the public good through representatives and civic virtue.

questions.prompt: The Declaration of Independence appeals to equality and natural rights. Which comparison best tests how fully those principles were applied in 1776?
choices: Compare its claims with contemporaneous laws and experiences of enslaved people, women, and Indigenous nations.
Treat its stated ideals as evidence that everyone immediately gained equal legal rights.
Ignore contemporaneous laws because political ideals cannot be studied historically.
Judge inclusion only by the number of printed copies.
questions.explanation: Comparing political ideals with law and lived experience reveals the limits and contested meanings of revolutionary liberty.

questions.prompt: A chart shows higher participation in boycotts after new British revenue measures. Which claim is most defensible?
choices: The pattern suggests coordinated colonial resistance but requires evidence before assigning one cause to every participant.
Every participant favored immediate independence from the outset.
Economic protest proves that all colonies shared identical interests.
The chart alone establishes how loyalists viewed parliamentary authority.
questions.explanation: Historical patterns can support an inference, but the motivations and varied positions of participants require corroboration.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least two specific pieces of evidence, answer: When colonists claimed natural rights, who was included, who was excluded, and why?
shortResponse.exemplar: A full-credit response states a defensible claim, uses two accurate details, explains how each supports the claim, and acknowledges one complexity or limitation.
